newsitem.title: USA: Plasma & Materials sees gain in chip speed.
newsitem.headline: Plasma & Materials sees gain in chip speed.

text.p: Plasma & Materials Technologies Inc said Monday it had made a breakthrough in the deposition of low dielectric constant materials that could significantly increase the speed of semiconductor devices.
The company, a supplier of etch and deposition equipment used to make semiconductors, said it will present its findings at a semiconductor industry conference in San Jose, Calif., today.
It said the new technique involves using a proprietary deposition technique that produces dielectric constant films that are two times lower than what is available currently.

As the number of transistors on a logic device increases, the complex scheme of interconnecting wiring and insulating layers has proven to be the bottleneck that limits the speed of the device, the company said.
Plasma & Materials said its breakthrough involves making high quality films with a dielectric constant of 2.0.

By contrast, other chip equipment makers have been able to achieve similar results in high density plasma (HDP) chemical vapor deposition (CVD) technology using fluorine as a dopant, but only down to a level of 3.2 to 3.5, the company said.
As a result, Plasma & Materials said it will focus all its Chemical Vapor Deposition resources to expand its Flowfill product line's development and evaluation efforts worldwide.
The system's ability to fill small gaps and simultaneously create a smooth planarized surface eliminates the need for Chemical Mechanical Planarization (CMP) on some devices.
The end result is increasing yields and a decrease in equipment costs, manufacturing time, and defect levels.
The sales price for Plasma & Materials' Flowfill Chemcial Vapor Deposition (CVD) ranges from about $1.4 million to $2.5 million, depending on configuration.
Plasma & Materials said the development was made at its recently acquired Electrotech unit.
